stories.title_en: A Cunning Broker Cheats on the Paper and Repays with His Daughter

paragraphs.en: Shi Shouxun was a native of Da'an in Fujian. His family was wealthy, and he regularly made paper to sell to merchants. One day he loaded more than a thousand baskets himself, worth over eight hundred taels, and went to Suzhou to sell them, lodging at the shop of the broker Weng Bin'er. Weng was an old hand among brokers and had piled up heavy debts to earlier clients. Seeing that Shi was a novice merchant, he used the entire shipment of paper to pay off those earlier clients, leaving Shi waiting for half a year. Shi's family then sent another five hundred-odd baskets of paper to Suzhou, and Weng sold them for him for cash. When the silver came in, he claimed it had gone to settle old accounts, and Shi waited another half a year. Realizing he had been strung along, Shi cursed him and beat him. Weng had no answer. With their fellow townsman Liu Guangqian mediating, Weng was made to write out an IOU for eight hundred taels, and Shi was advised to head home for the time being.

The next year Shi again shipped paper to Suzhou, and Weng sold it for cash. But the old debt remained hard to recover, so Shi waited in vain for another half-year. He noticed that Weng's daughter Yunying was good-looking and not yet betrothed. Thinking the silver would be difficult to collect, he asked Liu Guangqian to act as matchmaker and sought the daughter as a concubine to offset the debt. Weng happily agreed. The girl had just turned fifteen and flatly refused. Weng and his wife went in to press her: "In ancient times the girl Tiying offered to become a state slave to ransom her father from punishment. Now your father owes a client eight hundred taels of silver, and we are making it good with you. Besides, Fujian merchant families are often immensely rich; if you later bear a son and get a share of the family property, you will be set up in wealth here and enjoy no small fortune." Only then did the girl consent. Shi was already over sixty. They were married nearly four years; later Shi returned home and died. Before the mourning year was out, Weng remarried the girl as a concubine to Liang Enci of Lishui County, Nanjing, and collected another hundred taels in betrothal gifts.

When Shouxun's son Shi Qin learned of this, that same year he too shipped paper to Suzhou. He went to pay his respects at the Weng house and addressed Weng as "maternal grandfather." Weng ignored him. He asked for his stepmother to come out and see her; she too refused to come out. The other merchants there were angry and egged him on: "Your father paid eight hundred taels in betrothal gifts, they were man and wife only four years, and before the mourning period was over she was married off to another man. What harm would it do her to come out and see you once? The whole thing is outrageous! Why don't you report it to the authorities?" Qin then filed a complaint with the street-patrol censor Cai. By then Weng Bin'er, having gained Shi as a son-in-law, had restored the family fortunes and invested another thousand-plus taels in capital, so when the complaint came he felt not the slightest fear. Both sides enlisted backers, and the litigation dragged on nearly two years. Every office that handled the case took bribes and twisted the facts to decide it. Only when Qin filed with the Ministry of Justice did he get a fair judgment: "Weng Bin'er paid off eight hundred taels with his daughter — nearly the price of Lüzhu, the most costly concubine of old. But since Shouxun consented of his own accord, we will not go into the betrothal money. Now, before her husband's mourning period was complete, she was married off again to the merchant Liang, scooping up a second payment — this is treating a daughter as merchandise, with no regard for the law. He shall be beaten thirty strokes, and we award the body-price of one hundred taels, plus the fifty taels Shouxun spent on clothes and jewelry for Yunying, all to be paid over to Shi Qin." Because the lawsuits piled up year after year, Bin'er's family wealth was entirely drained, and he sank back into poverty.

Note: Of the harm done by swindles, the worst offenders are the bold rogues, and next the cunning brokers. The bold rogues set up schemes to cheat you in the dark—that is theft. The cunning brokers cheat you out of your goods and sell them openly—that is robbery. Both should be punished as bandits. As for the usual abuses of brokers: once a client's goods come into the shop, they lump them in to cover their debts, and they often skim off more for their own households; they habitually use a later client's goods to cover an earlier client's account. This is the normal state of a poor broker. Shi Shouxun's mistake was not sizing up the broker early on, so he fell into this pit. He should have pressed carefully for payment, or followed up with a lawsuit; he should not have schemed to take the daughter as a concubine. A man past sixty—how many years could he have left? Taking a concubine in a strange place—how could there not be trouble afterward? He left his son a lawsuit, and the costs were beyond counting. Though he won in the end, the gain did not cover the loss. What is hateful is Weng Bin'er, a heartless scoundrel: with one daughter he repaid eight hundred taels, already more than enough, and on top of that got a son-in-law's help to rebuild his household. Later, even when the girl remarried, he should have returned the body-price to Shi's son, and there would have been no trouble ever after. But his greedy heart was not satisfied, and he brought ruin on his house a second time. Truly this can serve as a warning mirror for those who cheat their conscience and betray what is right.

stories.title_en: A Poor Broker Gets Away with the Wax to Pay Old Debts

paragraphs.en: Zhang Ba was a native of Sichuan, shrewd and meticulous in his schemes, tall and strong. One day he bought over a hundred loads of wax and went to sell it at Qiu's shop in Jianning Prefecture, Fujian. This broker was stingy to the bone yet put on a wealthy appearance, owing vast sums of silver to previous clients. When Ba's wax arrived, the broker sent sharpers under false names to borrow the wax, promising to pay the silver later. A few days later, Ba strolled through the streets and found his wax spread across all the shops. When he asked for the buyers' names, none matched those on the account. Suspecting foul play, he returned to the shop and questioned the broker: "You have made off with my wax to settle old debts. Report every account truthfully. If you do not speak plainly, you will not escape a few punches." Broker Qiu fell silent. Ba swung his fists, pummeling him like a hawk seizing a sparrow, like kicking a ball about. Qiu hastily begged for mercy: "Sir, you are a god! That wax truly went to pay earlier clients' old accounts and for household use; how could I ask the shops to return it?" Zhang Ba said: "Write down what you repaid to people and what the shops bought, recording only that they borrowed it on credit and have not yet paid the silver. I will take this ledger to file a complaint, using you as my witness. Why should I fear the shops won't pay me again?" Qiu did as told and wrote out the delivery ledger item by item.

Zhang Ba then drew up a complaint and filed it with the prefecture. The acting prefect, Master Mei, read the complaint, threw it on the ground, and refused to accept it. Ba was heartsick at losing his capital and looked utterly crestfallen. After he pleaded again and again, Master Mei accepted the complaint. He first sent yamen runners to check the wax in the shops. Ba bribed the runners with silver, and they reported back: "The shops do indeed have wax bearing Zhang Ba's stamp." Master Mei said: "Who ever heard of taking a client's wax on credit and never paying the silver!" He at once issued a warrant to bring them in for trial.

The shops conferred among themselves outside: "Our shops bought merchant Zhang's wax and have already paid the silver; the broker received it. And the wax the broker used to repay us on his own account was the brokerage cut he was entitled to take. How can he now sue us over it a second time? Let us pool silver for the expenses, submit a portion as a bribe, explain our side first, and then face the trial." When the silver had been collected, they sent one hundred taels to a fellow townsman of Master Mei.

Master Mei, an upright official, would not listen to their pleas and ordered them brought in for trial. Among them was the man from the Jiang shop, a habitual litigant, who argued first: 'The wax was sold openly by Qiu the broker—a fair transaction. How can Zhang Ba demand payment again? Even if it wasn't fully paid, that is the broker's deduction—what does it have to do with us?' Qiu the broker replied: "The wax was not sold to them. I already owed old debts to the shops. When Zhang Ba's wax arrived, they falsely claimed they would borrow it and pay silver within a few days. Once they got the wax, they held onto it to offset the old debts. It is not that I dared to pocket the client's silver." Master Mei said: "If Qiu the broker owes debts, you must collect from him directly. How can you hold a client's goods to repay his debts? All of you will pay the price to Zhang Ba, and I will spare you punishment." The Jiang shop man, relying on his connections, argued repeatedly that it was a straightforward transaction with no debt offsetting. Master Mei grew angry and ordered him beaten ten strokes; when the man still refused to stop arguing, he was beaten twenty more. Then the others, terrified, all declared willingness to pay and begged for mercy. The Jiang man was imprisoned, while the rest secured guarantors. The wax money was assessed with a three-day deadline; if unpaid, they would be beaten again. Indeed, within three days, the full amount was collected. Ba received the silver and, deeply grateful for Master Mei's kindness, came before the hall carrying an incense burner in honor, kowtowed, and departed.

Note: When you go abroad to trade, a lone drifter in a land of few kin, you rely entirely on the broker as your eyes and ears. If you meet an honest broker, your goods have a master; once you fall in with a cunning one, your goods will be held back and your price cheated — that is certain. So choosing a broker is one of the great matters of trade; how can you not be careful? If a man's talk is straight and frank, he is an honest man. If at the first meeting he sizes you up and down and only then lets slip a few words, you can tell his mind is sly. If he names a price readily and it is not far off the mark, yet his replies are slow and halting, his heart must harbor deceit. If his house is finely built and fancier than it needs to be, he is usually a showy, extravagant man who cannot have saved much inside. If his clothes are patched and greasy, his look mean and his frame shabby, his shoulders hunched and his gaze shifty, his cap and kerchief out of season — these are all poor men. If he dresses in clever, outlandish ways and his colors are out of the ordinary, he is surely not a man who has built anything up, and he has no cash inside. If his cap and gown are plain and he wears only cloth, that is an honest, steady man; you cannot call him poor on that account. If a merchant knows this, how would he end up like Zhang Ba, having been made off with by a broker? And if the judge had not been the upright Master Mei but one willing to listen to backers, he would very nearly have gone home empty-handed. So I record this to show merchants: at the very start, when your goods are about to be released for sale, look carefully at the broker across from you; only then can you let the goods go and be sure of no mishap.
